text:
Quick SQL question for everyone…

We all use column aliases to make queries cleaner. But have you noticed this?

You can use an alias in ORDER BY, but you can’t use it in WHERE.

Example:

SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY annual_salary; -- works

But this fails:

SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
WHERE annual_salary > 500000; -- alias not allowed here

Why do you think SQL allows aliases in ORDER BY but not in WHERE?

Curious to hear everyone’s thoughts.

author: Sameer Khan
headline: Pursuing BE-IT At (RGIT) | Data Engineer
text:
🚀 What a Modern Data Engineer Actually Works 

People still think data engineering is just writing SQL and moving files around. It’s not.
Here’s a snapshot of the tools, languages, and platforms I regularly work with as a Data Engineer:

Languages:
1. Python (data processing, orchestration logic, APIs)
2. SQL (complex transformations, performance tuning)
3. Bash (automation, debugging pipelines)

Data & Storage:
PostgreSQL / MySQL
Snowflake / BigQuery / Redshift
Data Lakes on S3 / GCS / ADLS
Parquet, Avro, JSON
ETL / ELT & Orchestration
Apache Airflow
dbt (models, tests, documentation)
Custom Python pipelines

Streaming & Messaging:
Apache Kafka
Spark Structured Streaming
Big Data & Processing
Apache Spark (PySpark)
Databricks

Cloud & DevOps:
AWS / GCP / Azure
Docker
Kubernetes
Terraform

Data Quality & Monitoring:
Great Expectations
Custom data validation checks
Logging & alerting (CloudWatch / Stackdriver / Prometheus)

Version Control & CI/CD: 
Git (GitHub / GitLab)
CI/CD pipelines for data workflows
The real job?
Designing scalable pipelines
Fixing broken data at 2 AM
Optimizing costs and performance
Making data reliable enough that people actually trust it

If you’re learning data engineering and only focusing on tools without understanding data modeling, system design, and failure handling, you’re missing the point.
Build fundamentals. Tools change. Engineering principles don’t.
